title: How Should ADÉLA Build Off Her Debut Album’s Impressive Chart Debut?
summary: This week's Five Burning Questions looks at the No. 4 Billboard 200 bow of the Dream Academy alum's first full-length LP PRIMA.
contentText:
Though 2026 has been relatively slow in the minting of totally new pop stars, it appears one might be on the way with Slovak singer-songwriter ADÉLA.

The rising hitmaker — who first made public notice as a contest on the KATSEYE-forming reality contest show Dream Academy , then as an opener on Demi Lovato’s It’s Not That Deep tour — released her much-anticipated debut LP PRIMA on Sept. 4. On this week’s Billboard 200 (dated Sept. 19), the set bows at No. 4, while charting two singles in the Billboard Hot 100’s top 50: lead single “Ain’t in LA” (which moves 57-30) and follow-up “Nicole Kidman” (which debuts at No. 45).

How does her debut compare to our expectations? And what should she do next to take advantage of all of this? Billboard staffers and contributors answer these questions and more below.

1. ADÉLA’s  PRIMA  bows at No. 4 on the Billboard 200 this week with 56,000 first-week units. Is that first-week performance better, worse or about what you expected?

Lyndsey Havens : A bit better! I was expecting top 10, for sure, but once you remember that this album is home to her breakout hit and Hot 100 debut “Ain’t in LA” — plus “KGB” and “Red Bottoms” and latest single “Nicole Kidman” — it’s easy to see how it landed in the Billboard 200’s top 5.

Kristin Robinson : This is a little below what I expected. No. 4 is a very strong performance from a new artist, and she should be incredibly proud of that. That being said, I must be on the ADÉLA algorithm because, based on how much I’m seeing her song on TikTok, I actually thought this might be No. 2 or 3 this week. This just goes to show how much algorithms — or just a killer digital marketing campaign — can impact our perception of what is popular.

Andrew Unterberger : Higher! A debut in the back half of the top 10 would’ve still been a total success for ADÉLA on this campaign, given how new she still is and how many hitmakers feel permanently entrenched in the chart’s top five at this point. For her to get to No. 4 — well higher than recent efforts by more proven hitmakers like Karol G and Steve Lacy — is a real eye-opener.

Alicia Urrea : It’s about what I expected, but in the best way possible. As someone who has been watching ADÉLA’s transformation into the pop star she is now, I had a feeling PRIMA would have a very strong debut. The momentum around her has been building for some time, and the moment “Ain’t in LA” dropped, it felt like the beginning of a much bigger moment for her. A No. 4 debut with 56,000 units feels like a strong indication of where she is right now, and I think she has a growing fan base that is invested in her, but there’s also still room for her audience to expand. Considering how quickly her profile has grown, I think this is a very promising first-week result and, more importantly, a solid foundation for whatever is next.

Kristen Wisneski : It’s pretty much what I expected. For her second album, I think this is a great result. She’s put in the work, and it’s clearly paying off. I hope she continues to grow and get even bigger from here. Moving 56,000 units in her first week is a great achievement, and I think even more people will continue to discover her and become fans as she grows.

2. It seems like ADÉLA has recently received a massive surge of attention in a relatively short period of time — what do you see as being the biggest thing driving interest in her at the moment?

Lyndsey Havens : I think it’s been a series of right moves. Obviously, there’s a bit of a built-in fanbase having competed on Dream Academy . But more recently, she opened on tour for Demi Lovato, which cracked open that fanbase even wider. She followed that run by debuting on the Hot 100 with a single from her upcoming debut album, which never hurts. And then there’s the familiar beats of songs like “Ain’t in LA” and “Nicole Kidman,” which has only boosted familiarity for fans who hadn’t yet bought in. These are just pieces of the full package, though, which ADÉLA completes with her hot pink hair and open persona. She’s not trying to fit into any particular box, and as a result her album showcases a range of sounds and topics, and I think that’s what’s continuing to drive interest now — she got us hooked, then actually delivered.

Kristin Robinson : The biggest thing driving interest in her at the moment is TikTok. I am a new ADÉLA fan and I fell down the rabbit hole with “Ain’t In LA” — which has a great trend around, it where people will share some random place they are from and say, basically, “the baddest b–ches ain’t in LA.” All credit to her, though — she has followed up that song with “Nicole Kidman,” and I’m seeing that all over my feed too. I love the Nicole fan edits set to that song.

Andrew Unterberger : It feels like she’s already close to the complete package, in a way that pop fans are increasingly demanding from their hitmakers in 2026. It’s not enough to just be a good songwriter or performer or dancer, or to have good style or social media or overall branding — you kinda need all of it, and you need it right away. Whether due to her early training or good artistic development or just her innate pop talents — almost certainly a combination of the three — ADÉLA seems to have basically gotten there by the time of her first album. It’s a lot to ask of any young performer, but it’s right on time for pop stardom in 2026.

Alicia Urrea : I don’t think there’s one single thing driving ADÉLA’s rise, and I think that might be why it happened so quickly. There seems to be a real appetite for a new generation of female pop stars who have a strong sense of identity and empowerment, and ADÉLA has been able to position herself within that. Her team and label also deserve credit for giving her a recognizable visual identity with her pink hair and vibrant color palette. It makes her identifiable in a similar way to how Charli xcx’s green became inseparable from the Brat era.

But ultimately, the aesthetic only works because there’s an artist behind it. ADÉLA is genuinely talented as both a singer and a dancer, and she doesn’t seem to be treating those as separate parts of her artistry. Watching her lean equally into performance and vocals makes her feel like a fully formed pop artist, instead of someone who is simply benefitting from a viral moment.

Kristen Wisneski : She’s uniquely herself, and her story is so different from everyone else’s. She became popular through a group documentary, only to ultimately not be chosen. But instead of giving up, she continued pursuing her passion for singing and wanting this dream so badly that she found a way to stay in L.A. — even coming from outside the U.S.

I think so many fans admire her dedication and determination. She was even learning English while working the night shift! You can genuinely see how badly she wants this, and she’s such a powerhouse on stage. With her U.S. tour kicking off this week, I think people are going to get an even bigger glimpse of what she can do.

3. Breakthrough hit “Ain’t in LA” hits the Hot 100’s top 40 for the first time this week, bounding 57-30. Do you think it will keep climbing into the top 10 — something relatively few 2026 hits have managed to do — or will its momentum taper off before then?

Lyndsey Havens : I think that as we head into fall, it could taper off. It’s a fun, carefree and breezy song that came at the right time, and it makes sense that it would enjoy a post-album release bump, but I wouldn’t necessarily expect it to reach the top 10. 

Kristin Robinson : To me, it still has a good shot. I think her team at Capitol Records is really hungry to break her right…
